headline: Kizashi is the continuative stem of the verb 兆す (kizasu, “to show signs”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 兆(きざ)す (kizasu, “to show signs”).

headline: レンジ is borrowed from English range.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English range.

headline: Ōhaba is 大 (ō-, “large”) plus 幅 (haba, “width, breadth”).

sources.quote: Compound of 大(おお) (ō-, “large”) + 幅(はば) (haba, “width, breadth”).

headline: Kiryū is 気, air, plus 流, current or flow.

sources.quote: From 気, air, and 流, current/flow.

headline: Tsue is from Old Japanese and is found in the Man'yōshū.

sources.quote: ⟨tuwe⟩ → /tuwe/ → /t͡suwe/ → /t͡suje/ → /t͡sue/
From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

headline: Tsukuri is the continuative stem of the verb 作る (tsukuru, “to make, to produce, to manufacture”).

sources.quote: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 作る (tsukuru, “to make, to produce, to manufacture”).

headline: Kanbu is a calque of French cadre (“executive, manager”), from 幹 (kan, “core, main part”) plus 部 (bu, “division, department”).

sources.quote: Calque of French cadre (“executive, manager”), from 幹(かん) (kan, “core, main part”) + 部(ぶ) (bu, “division, department”).

headline: Mujaki is 無 (“non-”) plus 邪気 (“malice”), which occur in Classical Chinese but never as a single word.

sources.quote: 無 (“non-”) + 邪気 (“malice”), attestable in Classical Chinese e.g. Du Fu's famous prose 《秋述》 (literally “autumnal sentiments”) but never as a single word.

headline: Kerai was originally 家礼 (kerai).

sources.quote: Originally 家礼(けらい) (kerai).

headline: ペット is borrowed from English pet, and the source also lists clippings of トランペット (toranpetto, “trumpet”) and English PET.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English pet.
Abbreviation of トランペット (toranpetto, “trumpet”).
Borrowed from English PET, itself the initialism for polyethylene terephthalate, a common material used to make plastic.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wara.

headline: Oteage is 御 (o, honorific prefix) plus 手 (te, “hand, hands”) plus 上げ (age, “raising”), the stem of 上げる (ageru).

sources.quote: Compound of 御 (o, honorific prefix) + 手 (te, “hand, hands”) + 上げ (age, “raising”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 上げる ageru “to raise something”).

headline: In ikō, 向 is a daiyōji replacing 嚮.

sources.quote: 向 is a daiyōji replacing 嚮.
ikau > ikɔː > ikoː.

headline: Osu is 雄 (o, “male”) plus す (su), though the su is of unknown derivation.

sources.quote: /wosu/ → /osu/
Compound of 雄 (o, “male”) + す (su), but the derivation of the su element is unknown.
See also the etymology of 雌 (mesu).

headline: Michibiku is likely 道 (michi, “path”) plus 引く (hiku, “to pull; to draw”), meaning “to pull along a path”.

sources.quote: Likely formed from 道(みち) (michi, “path”) + 引(ひ)く (hiku, “to pull; to draw”, rendaku form 引(び)く (biku)), meaning "to pull along a path" -> "to lead/guide".

headline: Omonzuru shifted from Classical Japanese 重んず (omonzu), from 重 (omo, stem of 重い (omoi, “heavy”)) plus み plus す, literally “to treat as heavy”.

sources.quote: Regular shift in conjugation from Classical Japanese verb 重んず (omonzu), a phonetic shift from Classical Japanese 重みす (omomi su), from 重 (omo, stem of adjective 重い (omoi, “heavy”)) + み (-mi) + す (su, “to do”), where みす (-mi su) was a grammaticalised pattern meaning “treat (noun) as (adjective); find (noun) (adjective)”. Literally, “to treat as heavy”. Compare the kango (漢語) 重視 (jūshi, “value, esteem, respect”), from 重 (“heavy; important”) + 視 (“to see”).

meaning: to get confused, to be disordered, to be disturbed
headline: Midareru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic, and is compared with みだら (midara, “obscene, indecent”) and 乱す (midasu, “to disturb”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mintar-a-. Cognate with Okinawan 乱りゆん (njariyun).
Compare みだら (midara, “obscene, indecent”), 乱(みだ)す (midasu, “to disturb”), and 乱(みだ)りに (midari ni, “haphazardly, randomly”).

headline: Namari is perhaps related to Goguryeo 乃勿.

sources.quote: Perhaps related to Goguryeo 乃勿 (*namur). Compare Korean 납 (nap).
